extracted.intended_audience: students and writers (college-level) learning English sentence structure and revising for sentence variety
extracted.subtask_description: Identify subjects, verbs, clause connectors, and sentence patterns (simple, compound, complex, compound-complex) in prose, then revise for variety and clarity. The handout teaches how to find clause elements, recognize connector types and punctuation, and perform color-coding and editing exercises to improve sentence-level style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify subject and verb in a clause
rubrics_metrics.description: This handout: 'The subject shows who or what is doing the action... The verb shows the action or the state of being.' A clause is the combination of a subject and a verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find the subject (a noun or pronoun) and its verb first when analyzing sentences. Examples: 'Marvin slept.' 'Dogs bark.' Use subject/verb identification to determine clause boundaries and to analyze sentence structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize independent vs dependent clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent clause: 'a subject and verb that make a complete thought. Independent clauses are called independent because they can stand on their own and make sense.' Dependent clause: 'a subject and verb that don’t make a complete thought. Dependent clauses always need to be attached to an independent clause.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these definitions to decide whether a clause can stand alone. See the Writing Center handout on fragments for more detail. Remember dependent clauses are introduced by connectors and cannot stand alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect compound subjects and compound verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects and verbs can 'double up' in the same clause: 'Compound subject (two subjects related to the same verb)', 'Compound verb (two verbs related to the same subject)', and combinations thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify when multiple nouns share one verb or when one subject has multiple verbs. Note: 'You can tell that it’s only one clause because all of the subjects in one clause come before all of the verbs in the same clause.' Example: 'Javier, his colleagues, and their advisor drafted and revised the article several times.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple sentence (Pattern 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: One independent clause (SV.) — e.g., 'Mr. Potato Head eats monkeys.' 'I refuse.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scan your text to find sentences with only one clause. Mark them (the handout suggests using a color) so you can see how often you use simple sentences and whether you need to vary sentence length and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound sentence (Pattern 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more independent clauses. Arrangement options: (SV, and SV.) or (SV; however, SV.). Connectors include FANBOYS (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) and conjunctive adverbs with semicolons (however, moreover, nevertheless, nonetheless, therefore).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When identifying compound sentences, circle connectors and find the subject and verb of clauses on both sides. Pay attention to punctuation: use a comma with coordinating conjunctions (FANBOYS) and a semicolon plus comma with conjunctive adverbs. Examples: 'Mr. Potato Head eats them for breakfast every day, but I don’t see the attraction.' 'Eating them makes him happy; however, he can’t persuade me.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex sentence (Pattern 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: One independent clause plus one or more dependent clauses. Dependent-clause connectors are always at the beginning of the dependent clause and show relationships (cause/effect, comparison/contrast, place/manner, possibility/conditions, relation, time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn connector lists and their meanings: Cause/Effect (because, since, so that); Comparison/Contrast (although, even though, though, whereas, while); Place/Manner (where, wherever, how, however); Possibility/Conditions (if, whether, unless); Relation (that, which, who, whom); Time (after, as, before, since, when, whenever, while, until). Practice by circling complex connectors and finding the subject/verb that go with each connector. Watch for dependent clauses placed before, after, or embedded within the independent clause (e.g., 'Because SV, SV.' or 'S, because SV, V.').

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound-complex sentence (Pattern 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more independent clauses plus one or more dependent clauses. Uses connectors from Patterns 2 and 3 and can be arranged in multiple ways (e.g., 'SV, and SV because SV.' or 'Because SV, SV, but SV.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the connectors, then find the verbs and subjects that are part of each clause. Example: 'Mr. Potato Head said that he would share the secret recipe; however, if he does, Mrs. Potato Head will feed him to the piranhas, so we are both safer and happier if I don’t eat monkeys or steal recipes.' Use a distinct color to highlight compound-complex sentences to assess their frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use connectors appropriate to relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Connectors indicate how dependent clauses relate to independent clauses (e.g., cause/effect, comparison/contrast, place/manner, possibility/conditions, relation, time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose connectors that match the logical relationship you want to show (see the lists under Pattern 3). Using the wrong connector can obscure meaning; deliberate connector choice clarifies clause relationships and sentence flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation must match clause arrangement and connector type
rubrics_metrics.description: The handout notes: 'Notice how the punctuation changes with each arrangement.' Use commas with coordinating conjunctions (FANBOYS) and semicolon+comma for conjunctive adverbs; placement of dependent clauses affects comma usage (e.g., 'Because SV, SV.' vs 'SV because SV.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rearranging clauses, adjust punctuation accordingly. The punctuation rules shown (comma with FANBOYS; semicolon + conjunctive adverb + comma) are essential for grammatical compound and compound-complex sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze sentences by finding verbs and connectors first
rubrics_metrics.description: NOTE: 'Because nouns can fill so many positions in a sentence, it’s easier to analyze sentence patterns if you find the verbs and find the connectors.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start analysis with verbs and connectors rather than nouns to avoid confusion about clause roles. This method helps reveal clause boundaries and structure more reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and achieve sentence variety across the four patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: If you favor one particular pattern, 'your writing might be kind of boring if every sentence has exactly the same pattern.' The handout recommends checking the balance of the four patterns in your text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Color-code simple, compound, complex, and compound-complex sentences and examine the balance. Ask: Could you separate some complex sentences? Combine short sentences? Use different arrangements or connectors? Revise to improve rhythm and variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical revision exercises (scan/circle/highlight)
rubrics_metrics.description: The handout repeatedly instructs: 'Scan your own text to find the compound connectors... Circle them. Find the verb and the subject... Highlight your compound sentences with a color...' and similar steps for each pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use active, hands-on techniques—scanning for connectors, circling them, finding the associated subject/verb, and color-coding patterns—to diagnose overuse/underuse of patterns and guide sentence-level revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clause arrangement options affect emphasis and punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Patterns show arrangement options like '(SV because SV.)' or '(Because SV, SV.)' or '(S, because SV, V.)' indicating that dependent clauses can appear before, after, or interrupt independent clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When revising, experiment with clause position to change emphasis, flow, and rhythm. Remember to update punctuation whenever you change the clause order.
